The principal criminal statute protecting national defense information. It covers classic spying for a foreign power and also the unauthorized retention or disclosure of defense information by people who had lawful access to it.

::: {.official-links}
**Read the law** (official GovInfo text)

[Enacted text: 40 Stat. 217](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/statute/40/217){.btn-official} [Current U.S. Code: 18 U.S.C. 792-798](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/18/793?link-type=html){.btn-official}
:::

## Key provisions

- 18 U.S.C. 793: gathering, transmitting, retaining, or losing national defense information.
- 18 U.S.C. 794: delivering defense information to a foreign government, punishable by life imprisonment or death.
- 18 U.S.C. 798: disclosure of classified communications intelligence and cryptographic information.

## Why it matters

The act predates the classification system and never mentions it, speaking instead of 'information relating to the national defense'. That mismatch drives most of the controversy over its use against leakers and over mishandling cases. Prosecutions rely on [CIPA](cipa-1980.qmd) to manage classified evidence.

## Current status

In force. The 1918 Sedition Act amendments were repealed in 1921; section 798 on communications intelligence was added in 1950.

## Where it sits

- **Layer.** Framework statute. Standing laws that create institutions or general procedures other laws and executive actions plug into, such as the National Security Act, the War Powers Resolution, IEEPA, and FISA. ([How the layers work](../study/index.qmd#the-authority-stack))
- **Era.** Civil War to the First World War ([timeline](../study/timeline.qmd)).
- **Study.** [Unit 5: Intelligence and its oversight](../study/units/intelligence-oversight.qmd) (core reading).
